title: Pick Two?
setting: a town cut off by a storm

post.author: u/forecourt_myfanwy
post.title: I run the night shift at a mountain town's only fuel station. A storm cut our line for 7.5 hours, and an account with £120 in it paid for £225 of fuel.

blocks.text: I'm Myfanwy, night attendant at the only fuel station in Cwmhelyg, a mountain town at the top of the pass. Most trade is on the region's fuel cards: a business gets one card per driver, and every card spends from its one account. The balances live on a computer at head office, in the city, 140 km down the valley.

A phone line runs down to head office. While it's up, the till asks before every card sale: it sends the card and amount, and head office checks the balance, takes the sale off and answers yes or no. That takes about 400 ms (milliseconds, thousandths of a second).
Every hour the till also syncs: it sends head office any sales it's holding, then copies every balance into its own list. So its list trails head office by up to an hour.

When the line is down, the till is offline: it can't reach head office. Storms have cut our line before. The old rule was a cap: each card could spend at most £25 until the line came back; bigger sales were refused. Drivers complained £25 doesn't fill a plough.

On Monday 14 December an update changed the rule. Now, offline, the till keeps selling up to the last known balance: the balance it copied at its last sync. In steps: it checks its list, approves the sale if it fits, takes it off the list, and stores it to send later.
Each stored sale carries the time on the till's clock, called its timestamp.

On Friday 15 January the storm took the line down at 21:40, for 7.5 hours, the longest cut I've known. Cwmhelyg and the city became two halves that couldn't hear each other. In the trade that's a partition: a cut between parts of one system. My list wasn't trailing any more. It was alone.

Cynfael's firm keeps the pass road open. On storm nights one plough works up from the city, one down from here, and they meet halfway. Both drivers carry cards on the same account, which Cynfael tops up on Fridays. That night it held £120.
At 00:18 Iestyn pulled in with the town plough and asked for £110. My till showed £120 available, its last known balance from the 21:00 sync. Approved. Stored.

At 00:31, 140 km away, Aneurin filled the city plough at the card company's depot. Its line was fine, so it asked head office, which still had £120: Iestyn's sale was sitting in my till, unheard. Approved: £115.

At 05:10 the line came back and the till settled up, in three steps. It sent its stored sales. Head office applied them in order of time. Then it flagged every account below zero, and the slip printer started chattering. Head office calls this reconciliation.
The slip, line by line: time, place, driver, sale, what happened, and the balance at head office after it.

00:18  Cwmhelyg till  Iestyn   £110  stored offline      balance £120
00:31  city depot     Aneurin  £115  approved online     balance £5
05:10  Cwmhelyg till  Iestyn   £110  applied from store   balance -£105  BELOW ZERO, FLAGGED
Two ploughs. One account. £225 of fuel on £120.

diagram.aria: The night from 21:00 to 05:30. Row one, the valley line: up until 21:40, cut for 7.5 hours, back at 05:10. Row two, the Cwmhelyg till: Iestyn's 110 pound sale at 00:18, then stored and unheard until 05:10. Row three, the city depot: Aneurin's 115 pound sale at 00:31. Iestyn's £110 at 00:18 sat in my till, unheard, until the line came back. Aneurin's £115 at the city depot at 00:31 went straight to head office, which still had £120 and left £5. At 05:10 the stored sale reached head office and the slip printed -£105.

blocks.text: Nobody cheated: two machines that couldn't hear each other both said £120. The next storm is forecast for Thursday 21 January. What should we change?

comments.author: u/grey_pager
comments.text: Two halves that can't talk still get asked questions. A copy that answers only when it agrees with the one true balance is called consistent. A copy that answers every request with whatever it has is called available. Before you choose, read your slip again. While the line was cut, which sales could anyone check against the true balance? How much did your till approve that head office never saw, and what set that amount? And with the line up, what does each sale pay for being sure?

replies.author: u/forecourt_myfanwy
replies.text: Checked against the true balance: only Aneurin's, at the depot. Mine couldn't be. Unseen by head office: £110, all of Iestyn's, and the rule set it: whatever my list said. And with the line up, every sale waits about 400 ms for its yes.

comments.author: u/pick_two_eadgyth
comments.text: This is the CAP theorem, short for consistency, availability and partition tolerance (keeping going while the line is cut). Pick two. A town in a storm can't lose its till, so pick availability and give up consistency. Keep selling to the last known balance. When the line comes back, sort out any clash, two sales that spent the same money, by timestamp: keep the newer sale and drop the older one. It runs itself, and nobody has to phone anyone at dawn.

replies.author: u/forecourt_myfanwy
replies.text: Head office's night manager likes this one. No refusals, and the merge runs itself.

comments.author: u/no_line_no_sale_torborg
comments.text: I counted cash for a bank most of my working life. If you can't check the money, don't take the card. Refuse every card sale until the line is back, and not one account goes below zero. A queue in the snow is cheaper than a debt.

reply.prompt: The next storm is forecast for Thursday 21 January. What should head office change in the till before then? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Offline, let each card spend up to a small cap, refuse bigger sales, settle after.
options.part2: On Wednesday 20 January head office changed the rule one kind of operation at a time. Fuel on a card while offline: up to £25 per card for the whole cut, bigger sales refused. Top-ups, where a firm adds money to its account at my counter, refused while offline: they wait for head office. With the line up: ask head office first, as before. When the line returns: send the stored sales, apply them in order of time, flag anything below zero. In the sim, replaying 15 January with the cap: Iestyn's £110 is refused and he takes the £25 the cap allows; Aneurin's £115 is approved at the depot; at 05:10 the slip shows -£20, flagged. Never more than £25 at risk on his card. On Thursday the storm cut the line again. The ploughs got small fills, the pass stayed open, and the dawn slip needed a phone call, not a meeting.
options.senior: CAP doesn't let you pick two once for the whole system; it says that during a cut, each operation that needs the far side must refuse or answer with what it has. So choose per operation and put a number on the risk. Small fills are worth answering offline up to a cap per card, the way card terminals use a floor limit; big sales and changes to the account wait for the line. Settle afterwards in order and flag what went below zero for a person. The cap is the most you have chosen to lose on one card.

options.text: Refuse every card sale while the line is down, so no account can ever be overspent.
options.part2: On Wednesday 20 January head office set the till to refuse every card sale while offline. In the sim, replaying 15 January: Iestyn's £110 is refused; card fuel sold in town, £0; Aneurin's £115 is approved at the depot; nothing is stored, no slip, nothing below zero. On Thursday the storm cut the line again. Iestyn's plough stood at my pumps with an empty tank until the line came back, and the town side of the pass stayed shut till morning.
options.senior: Refusing everything while cut off is the consistent choice, and it is honest: no account can ever go below zero. It is the right rule for operations that can't be undone or are worth a lot, like top-ups or account changes. But applied to every operation, it turns a cut line into a closed station, and in a storm the cost of no fuel is a road nobody can clear. Keep refusal for the operations that need it, and bound the rest with a cap.

options.text: Sync the till with head office more often while the line is up, so balances are fresh.
options.part2: On Wednesday 20 January head office set the till to sync every 5 minutes. In the sim, replaying 15 January: the till's last copy is from 21:35 instead of 21:00, and it still says £120, because nothing moved on the account before the cut. Iestyn's £110 is approved offline, Aneurin's £115 is approved at the depot, and at 05:10 the slip shows -£105, flagged. A fresher copy is still a copy, and during the cut it can't get any fresher.
options.senior: Syncing more often shrinks how far the till's list trails head office while the line is up. That is replication lag, and it matters on a normal night. But tonight's problem wasn't lag. It was a partition: both sides kept spending after the last sync, and no sync crosses a cut line. More frequent syncs can't change what happens during the cut; only the rule for each operation can.

options.text: Keep selling up to the last known balance, and let the newest timestamp settle clashes.
options.verdict: A clean slip, a hidden loss
options.part2: On Wednesday 20 January head office kept the rule and added the merge: when two sales spent the same money, the newer timestamp stays and the older is dropped. In the sim, replaying 15 January: both sales are approved, and at 05:10 Iestyn's 00:18 sale clashes with Aneurin's at 00:31. The newer one stays. The slip shows £5, nothing flagged, and £110 of fuel is never charged to anyone. Thursday's slip came out clean too. That's what worried me.
options.senior: Both sales happened: the fuel is in two tanks. A merge that keeps the newer timestamp can't undo a sale, it can only drop it from the record, so the loss is still there and nobody is told. It also trusts the clock of a till that was cut off for 7.5 hours, which is Rule 6: never trust the clock on the wall. Settling must keep every sale, apply them in order and flag the hole for a person; the offline rule must bound how big the hole can get.

sim.title: Replay the night the valley line was cut
sim.lede: You're Myfanwy on Friday 15 January 2027 at 21:00, before the line goes down. As given data: Cynfael's account holds £120 at head office, and the till copies every balance at each sync while the line is up (every 60 minutes from 21:00). The storm cuts the line from 21:40 to 05:10. At 00:18 Iestyn asks for £110 in town; at 00:31 Aneurin asks for £115 at the city depot, which is always online and asks head office. Asking head office first takes about 400 ms a sale. The cap, where used, is £25 per card for the whole cut; a driver refused by the cap takes what it allows. When the line returns, the till sends its stored sales and head office settles them. Set the rules, then play 21:00 to 05:30.
sim.tryThis: Try this: play it as built: both sales approved, the slip shows -£105, £110 at risk. Cap of £25: Iestyn's £110 refused, he takes £25, the slip shows -£20. Refuse every card sale: £0 of card fuel in town, no slip. Sync every 5 minutes: last copy at 21:35, still £120, slip still -£105. Newest timestamp wins: the slip shows £5, but £110 of fuel is never charged. No cut and asking first: Iestyn waits 400 ms and Aneurin is refused. No cut and no asking, hourly sync: -£105 with no storm at all.

explain.oneLine: Nothing at head office broke. For 7.5 hours the town till and head office were two halves of one system that couldn't hear each other, and the till's rule answered every sale with what it had, the last known balance. Both halves spent the same £120. During a cut each operation must choose: refuse, or answer and settle later, with a risk you have chosen in advance.

steps.title: A cut forces a choice, one operation at a time.
steps.text: A partition is a cut between parts of one system: messages from one side never reach the other. Here the town till and head office were the two sides from 21:40 to 05:10. During a cut, a request that needs the other side has two honest answers. First, refuse or wait until the line returns: every answer agrees with the one true balance, so the system stays consistent, but it is not available. Second, answer with what this side has: it stays available, but its copy may be wrong. There is no third answer, because nothing crosses the cut. That is what CAP says, honestly: not 'pick two for ever', but 'while cut off, each operation chooses'. With no cut, a system can be both. What goes wrong: treating partition tolerance as optional. Storms and diggers decide that, not designers.

steps.title: Offline approval, step by step.
steps.text: First, the till copies each account's balance at every sync. Second, when the line drops, it approves a sale if it fits that copy, the last known balance. Third, it takes the sale off its copy and stores it with a timestamp. Fourth, it sends the stored sales when the line returns. What goes wrong at the second step: the copy only knows the till's own sales. Head office, still online, keeps approving against its own balance, and neither side hears the other. On 15 January both said £120, so £225 was approved on £120. A fresher copy before the cut changes nothing: syncing every 5 minutes moves the last copy to 21:35, still £120, because the money moved after the cut.

steps.title: Settling up when the line returns.
steps.text: Reconciliation is three steps. First, the till sends every stored sale. Second, head office applies them to the true balance in order of time. Third, it flags any account below zero, so a person can chase it, and the slip prints. What goes wrong at the second step: a merge that settles clashes by the newest timestamp. Both sales already happened and the fuel is in two tanks, so dropping one doesn't undo it, it hides it: the slip reads £5 and £110 of fuel is never charged. The timestamps also come from a till cut off for hours, and Rule 6 says never trust the clock on the wall. Settling must keep every sale and flag the hole.

steps.title: A small cap bounds the loss.
steps.text: The fix is a choice per operation, not one rule for the whole till. A small fuel sale may be answered offline, up to a cap per card for the whole cut. A bigger sale is refused until the line returns. Anything that changes the account itself, like a top-up, waits for head office. The cap is the most you can lose on one card, chosen in advance: with £25, Iestyn's £110 is refused, he takes £25, and the slip shows -£20. Card terminals work the same way with a floor limit: below it a terminal may approve offline and send the sale later; above it, the terminal won't approve offline. What goes wrong: a cap per card on an account with many cards. Set a limit per account too.

steps.title: PACELC: the choice when nothing is cut.
steps.text: PACELC adds the everyday half: if there is a partition (P), choose availability (A) or consistency (C); else (E), choose latency (L), the wait for an answer, or consistency (C). Cwmhelyg's till chooses consistency while the line is up: it asks head office before every sale and waits about 400 ms. Turning that off, approving on the till's own list and syncing hourly, saves the wait but lets 15 January's sums happen with no storm at all: Iestyn approved on the list at 00:18, Aneurin at head office at 00:31, and the 01:00 sync prints -£105. Syncing every 5 minutes settles Iestyn's sale at 00:20 and Aneurin is refused. What goes wrong: forgetting the wait is paid on every sale, every day, not only in storms.

diagram.aria: The fix replayed for 15 January. At 21:40 the line is cut and the till goes offline with a cap of 25 pounds per card. At 00:18 Iestyn asks for 110 pounds; the till refuses it as over the cap, and he takes 25 pounds, stored. At 00:31 the city depot asks head office for Aneurin's 115 pounds, approved, leaving 5 pounds. At 05:10 the till sends the stored 25 pounds. Outcome: the slip shows minus 20 pounds, flagged.

explain.caption: The fix, replayed for 15 January. While the line is cut, the till answers small fills up to £25 a card and refuses bigger sales. Iestyn takes £25; Aneurin's £115 goes through at the depot; at 05:10 the stored £25 is settled and the slip shows -£20, flagged. The risk was chosen in advance: at most £25 on his card.

fix.title: The fix: choose per operation, cap small offline sales, settle and flag after
fix.text: Make the offline rule a choice per kind of operation, not one rule for the whole till. Fuel on a card: allowed offline up to £25 per card for the whole cut; bigger sales refused until the line returns. Top-ups and anything else that changes an account: refused offline, they wait for head office. With the line up: keep asking head office first, about 400 ms a sale. When the line returns: send the stored sales, apply them in order of time, flag any account below zero for a person to chase, and never drop a sale to make the sums tidy. For accounts with many cards, add an offline limit for the whole account as well.

limits: A cap per card bounds one card, not one account. An account with many cards can lose a cap on each, so set a limit per account too.
A cap doesn't stop an account going below zero; it bounds how far. Settling only finds the debt, and someone still has to chase it.
Asking head office first while the line is up costs about 400 ms a sale. If the line is slow, that wait grows on every sale, and the choice between waiting and being sure comes back.

head: Rule while the line is cut
Good
Bad
rows: Both halves spend the same £120: slip -£105, £110 at risk.
£0 of card fuel in town; the town plough waits for the line.
A fresher copy before the cut (21:35, not 21:00).
During the cut it changes nothing: slip still -£105.
£110 of fuel never charged; trusts a cut-off till's clock.
£25 cap per card, bigger sales refused, settle and flag
Small fills keep going; at most £25 at risk on a card: slip -£20.
A debt to chase; big jobs wait for the line.

explain.seniorTake: CAP is not a menu you pick from once. A partition happens to you, and while it lasts every operation that needs the far side has two honest answers: refuse and stay correct, or answer with your own copy and accept being wrong for a while. So decide per operation, and put a number on how wrong you can afford to be. Small, frequent, low-harm actions, like a £25 fill, can be answered offline up to a cap and settled later; big or hard-to-undo ones, like a £110 fill or a top-up, wait. Settling keeps every sale, applies them in order and flags what went below zero for a person; a merge that drops one side by timestamp only hides the loss. And when nothing is cut, PACELC's question remains: each sale pays about 400 ms to be sure. Pay it where money changes hands.

realWorld.title: Brewer, 2000: the conjecture
realWorld.text: Eric Brewer's keynote slides from PODC, 19 July 2000, name consistency, availability and tolerance to network partitions, then say: "Theorem: You can have at most two of these properties for any shared-data system". An earlier slide, comparing strict and relaxed systems, adds: "But I think it’s a spectrum".

realWorld.title: Brewer: disconnected clients
realWorld.text: Among his "CAP Take Homes": "Disconnected clients can’t have both". A till whose line is cut is a disconnected client: it can have consistency or availability for each sale, not both.

realWorld.title: Gilbert and Lynch, 2002: the proof
realWorld.text: Seth Gilbert and Nancy Lynch turned Brewer's conjecture into a proof. Their abstract: "It is impossible to achieve all three." Their availability is strict: "every request received by a non-failing node in the system must result in a response." A node is one machine, like Cwmhelyg's till.

realWorld.title: Gilbert and Lynch: the best known value
realWorld.text: Their practical way out times out a lost message and answers locally: "The client is then sent a response: either the best known value of the local node (for a read operation), or an acknowledgment (for a write operation). In this case, atomic consistency may be violated." The till's last known balance is exactly a best known value.

realWorld.title: Abadi, 2012: CAP is for failures
realWorld.text: Daniel Abadi writes: "In reality, CAP only posits limitations in the face of certain types of failures, and does not constrain any system capabilities during normal operation."

realWorld.title: Abadi: PACELC
realWorld.text: His fuller question: "if there is a partition (P), how does the system trade off availability and consistency (A and C); else (E), when the system is running normally in the absence of partitions, how does the system trade off latency (L) and consistency (C)?" At Cwmhelyg the latency is about 400 ms a sale.

realWorld.title: Adyen: an offline limit per sale
realWorld.text: Adyen's point-of-sale docs describe the limit their card terminals use offline: "This is a maximum per-transaction amount that your terminals or the Mobile SDK can approve while offline." And what happens to an approved sale: "If approved, the terminal or Mobile SDK stores the card data and details of the transaction."

asked: Design a payment terminal that works offline.
interview.answer: CAP is about what happens during a partition: a cut between parts of a system that messages can't cross. You don't get to choose whether partitions happen; cables and storms do. While the cut lasts, any request that needs the far side has two honest answers: refuse, and every answer stays consistent with the one true copy; or answer with your own copy, and stay available but possibly wrong. There is no third, because nothing crosses the cut. With no cut, you can have both. And the choice is per operation, not per system. PACELC adds the everyday half: else, when nothing is cut, you still trade latency, the wait to ask the true copy, against consistency. For an offline payment terminal I'd design it per operation. With the line up, ask the bank or head office first and pay the wait. With the line down, approve small payments offline up to a floor limit per card, and a limit per account, refuse bigger ones, and refuse anything that changes the account. Store each offline sale with its card and amount, send them when the line returns, apply them in order and flag any that leave an account below zero for a person. Never settle clashes by timestamp, because both sales happened. I'd tell the story of a mountain fuel station whose till sold £110 offline to the last known balance of £120 while the city depot, still online, sold £115 from the same account: the slip at 05:10 said -£105. With a £25 cap, the same night ends at -£20, a loss chosen in advance.

atWork: Look for places where one offline rule covers every operation. A common pattern is a shop till, a mobile app or a branch server that keeps working while cut off from the main database, with a single switch: either everything is refused, or everything is accepted against a local copy and merged later. Read-only access is enough. First, list the operations that can happen while cut off: reads, small payments, big payments, refunds, account changes. For each, decide refuse or answer, and if answer, the most you can lose, as a cap per user and per account. Second, read how the merge works when the connection returns: does it keep every operation, apply them in order and flag problems for a person, or does it drop one side by timestamp? Third, measure what asking the main copy first costs when nothing is cut, and on which operations you pay it. In AWS, check how any table you replicate across regions settles writes made on both sides of a cut, and how your mobile apps queue actions while offline. This per-operation choice, refuse or accept up to a limit and settle later, is the behaviour Build Night L7 (Zones, regions and partitions) asks you to model; it unlocks after s8e01, s8e04 and s8e06. Standards: if your company is pursuing ISO/IEC 27001:2022, Annex A 5.30 (ICT readiness for business continuity) expects you to plan how services keep running through a disruption such as a cut line, and an offline mode with written limits and a reconciliation step is evidence of that plan. Flag for the design: a single offline rule with no per-operation limits, or a merge that silently drops operations, would need rework before an audit, so write each operation's choice and its limit into the design from the first draft.

recall.prompt: A café's card reader loses its connection to the bank on a busy Saturday. The owner wants it to keep taking cards with no risk at all. What can you honestly promise, and what would you set up?

keyIdeas.idea: While cut off, each payment must be either refused or approved without the bank, so 'always take cards' and 'no risk' can't both hold
Approve small payments offline up to a set limit per card, and refuse bigger ones
Store the offline payments and settle them when the line returns, chasing any that fail

recall.model: I can't promise both. While the reader is cut off from the bank, each payment must be either refused or approved without checking, so 'always take cards' and 'no risk' can't both hold during the cut; that is all CAP says. What I can promise is a small, chosen risk. Set a floor limit: approve small payments offline, up to a cap per card for the whole outage, and refuse bigger ones until the line is back. Store each offline payment and settle them when the line returns, in order, and chase any that the bank declines. The cap is the most the café can lose on one card, and the owner picks it.

recall.prompt: In the sim, with the line cut and everything else as built, which offline rule still sells card fuel in town and keeps the slip no more than £25 below zero?
options: Keep selling to the last known balance
A cap of £25 per card, bigger sales refused
Last known balance, with a sync every 5 minutes
recall.why: With the cap, Iestyn's £110 is refused and he takes £25; Aneurin's £115 is approved at the depot; at 05:10 the slip shows -£20. The last known balance gives -£105 whatever the sync interval, and refusing every card sale sells no card fuel in town at all.

recall.prompt: What does PACELC add to CAP?
options: A fourth property to pick instead of partition tolerance
The choice when nothing is cut: wait for the sure answer, or answer faster and risk being wrong
Proof that every system must give up one property for ever
A rule that the newest timestamp wins after a cut
recall.why: CAP only speaks about a partition. PACELC adds the else: even with no cut, asking the one true copy first costs latency, about 400 ms a sale at Cwmhelyg, so each operation trades waiting against being sure.

recall.prompt: In an interview you're asked to explain CAP without saying 'pick two'. What do you say?

keyIdeas.idea: A partition is a cut that messages can't cross, and it isn't optional
During it, each request either refuses (consistent) or answers with its own copy (available), which may be wrong
The choice is per operation and only during the cut; with no cut, PACELC's latency trade-off applies

recall.model: CAP is about what happens during a partition: a cut between parts of a system that messages can't cross. You don't choose whether partitions happen; cables and storms do. While the cut lasts, any request that needs the far side must refuse or answer. Refusing keeps every answer consistent with the one true copy; answering with its own copy keeps it available, but the answer may be wrong. There is no third option, because nothing crosses the cut. With no cut, a system can be both. And the choice is per operation: a small fuel sale can be answered offline up to a cap, a big one refused. PACELC adds the rest: else, when nothing is cut, you still trade latency, the wait to ask the true copy, against consistency.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 3 months later. The cap has held all winter: small fills in every storm, and slips that need a phone call, not a meeting. Then on Friday 19 March 2027 the line went down from 22:10 to 03:40. A timber haulier's account held £40. His six drivers each filled up here that night, £25 apiece, every sale within the cap. At 03:40 the slip printed: -£110, flagged.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to Myfanwy. Every sale obeyed the £25 cap, so how did one account end £110 below zero, and what should change?

keyIdeas.idea: The cap is per card, and the account had six cards, so its offline risk was six caps
Add an offline limit for the whole account, shared across all its cards
Keep settling up in order and flagging, and size the limits to what you can afford to lose

coldCase.model: The cap is per card, and the haulier's account has six cards, so offline it could lose six caps: six drivers each took £25, £150 against £40, and the slip shows -£110. Each card obeyed its cap; the account had no limit of its own. Add an offline limit per account, shared across all its cards, so the whole account can't spend more than a set amount that head office hasn't seen, and keep the per-card cap under it. Keep settling up in order and flag the account so someone can chase the debt. The limits are how much you can afford to lose on one account while the line is down, so choose them for the biggest accounts, not the average one.
